lessons.title: License Raj Inflation: India's High-Inflation, Low-Growth Decades

children.text: Today, if you have the money, you can order a phone on Flipkart and have it delivered tomorrow, or open a Zerodha account and buy a stock on the NSE within minutes. For much of the three decades before 1991, having the money was not the constraint. Buying a Bajaj scooter or a Premier Padmini car in India often meant joining a waiting list years long, regardless of how much cash you had in hand, because the manufacturer needed a government license just to produce more units. That single fact, money available but supply legally capped, is the key to understanding why India ran chronically high inflation for decades without ever having a single dramatic hyperinflation moment like Weimar Germany.

body.text: License Raj inflation was not one shock, it was a chronic structural regime: a fiscal deficit the RBI routinely financed by printing money, a supply side permanently shackled by licensing rules, and periodic droughts, wars and oil shocks landing on a system too rigid to respond.

children.text: Under the Industries (Development and Regulation) Act of 1951 and the Five-Year Plans that followed, setting up or expanding almost any significant industrial business in India required a government license. The policy aimed to build domestic industry through import substitution and to steer investment toward planners' priorities rather than the market's. In practice, it also meant that even a wildly profitable, clearly in-demand business could not simply expand production to meet demand, it had to wait for bureaucratic approval, which could take years. The Monopolies and Restrictive Trade Practices (MRTP) Act of 1969 added a further layer, deliberately restricting large, established firms from growing further, in the name of preventing concentration of economic power.

body.text: Economist Raj Krishna coined the term "Hindu rate of growth" to describe India's average GDP growth of roughly 3.5% a year across the 1950s through the 1980s, a rate far below what comparable Asian economies achieved over the same decades. The License Raj is widely seen as a central cause: capital and enterprise existed, but the regulatory system throttled how fast supply could actually grow.

children.text: The Monetary Engine, in Slow Motion

For most of this era, the RBI did not operate as an independent inflation-fighter the way it does today under the flexible inflation-targeting framework you met in Chapter 1. Government deficits were routinely financed through ad hoc Treasury Bills that the RBI was effectively obligated to purchase, a practice often described as automatic monetization: the government spent more than it collected in taxes, and the RBI created new money to cover the gap, more or less on demand. This is the same monetary engine behind Weimar Germany's hyperinflation from Chapter 2, just running at a far slower, chronic simmer rather than an explosive boil. This arrangement was not phased out until an agreement between the RBI and the government in the mid-1990s replaced it with a more disciplined Ways and Means Advances system by 1997, well after the crisis covered in the next lesson.
A Supply Side That Could Not Respond

Chapter 1 gave you three engines: demand-pull, cost-push, and monetary. License Raj India adds a variant worth naming on its own: regulatory supply rigidity. In a normal cost-push shock, like the 1973 oil embargo, prices eventually stabilise once supply adjusts, once alternative energy sources are found, production shifts, or the shock simply fades. In License Raj India, supply frequently could not adjust even when firms wanted it to, because expansion itself required a permit that might not arrive for years. That turned what should have been temporary shocks, a bad monsoon, a spike in import costs, into much longer-lasting price pressure, because the usual release valve, businesses expanding output to meet demand, was regulated shut.

body.title: Three Decades of Recurring Shocks on a Rigid System

events.title: War and Drought Together
events.description: The 1965 war with Pakistan strains government finances just as a severe drought hits food production, draining foreign exchange reserves and pushing food prices up sharply.

events.title: The Rupee Is Devalued
events.description: Facing a foreign exchange crisis, India devalues the rupee by roughly 36%, from about 4.76 to 7.50 per US dollar. The move is deeply unpopular domestically and, combined with the drought, is widely cited as pushing wholesale inflation into the low teens that year.

events.title: Bank Nationalisation
events.description: The government nationalises 14 major banks in 1969 and 6 more in 1980, aiming to direct credit toward priority sectors, but also tightening the government's grip on how credit and money creation flowed through the economy.

events.title: Oil Shock Meets Drought
events.description: The global oil embargo from Chapter 2 hits an already import-dependent India alongside a poor monsoon. Wholesale price inflation is widely cited as approaching 25% that year, one of the most severe inflationary episodes in independent India's history.

events.title: The Second Oil Shock, Again
events.description: A further drought and the second global oil shock push Indian inflation back into double digits, adding to two decades of recurring, structurally-entrenched price pressure.

body.title: Money in Hand, Nothing to Buy
body.scenario: A Mumbai family in the 1970s has saved enough to buy a scooter. The waiting list for a new Bajaj scooter is several years long, because Bajaj's production capacity is capped by its industrial license and it cannot simply build a new plant to meet demand. Grey-market scooters, resold ahead of the queue, trade at a significant premium over the official price.
body.prompt: Which of the three engines from Chapter 1, demand-pull, cost-push, or monetary, best explains the price premium on grey-market scooters, and why doesn't the usual textbook fix (the manufacturer simply produces more) work here?
body.modelAnswer: The underlying pressure has genuine demand-pull characteristics, the family has real purchasing power and wants to buy, but the textbook demand-pull fix, businesses expanding supply until the shortage clears, is blocked by regulation rather than by any real production constraint. This is the regulatory supply rigidity this lesson adds to the framework: demand-side pressure that cannot resolve itself through normal supply expansion because the constraint is legal, not economic. The grey-market premium is essentially the price of jumping the queue that licensing created.

body.title: Quick Check
body.question: Why is License Raj inflation described in this lesson as "the monetary engine in slow motion" rather than a sudden hyperinflation like Weimar Germany?
options: India's government ran budget surpluses throughout this period
The RBI's automatic, ad hoc financing of government deficits created chronic, ongoing money creation, but at a far slower pace than Weimar's runaway printing
India had no central bank during this period
India's currency was fully convertible into gold throughout this era
body.explanation: The mechanism, government deficits financed by the central bank creating money, is genuinely the same monetary engine as Weimar Germany's. The difference is scale and speed: India's deficits and the resulting money creation were chronic and moderate rather than explosive, producing persistent high inflation over decades rather than hyperinflation in months.

points: License Raj inflation was chronic and structural, not a single shock: a routinely-monetized fiscal deficit, a supply side capped by industrial licensing, and recurring droughts, wars and oil shocks hitting a rigid system.

The License Raj adds a variant to the three engines from Chapter 1: regulatory supply rigidity, where even genuine demand-pull pressure cannot resolve itself because expanding supply required a government permit.
The RBI's ad hoc, near-automatic financing of government deficits through this era is the same monetary mechanism behind Weimar Germany's hyperinflation, just running at a much slower, chronic pace.

Recurring shocks, the 1966 devaluation, the 1973-74 oil shock and drought, and the 1979-80 repeat, layered on top of this rigid system rather than resolving cleanly the way a freer economy's shocks tend to.
By the late 1980s, decades of deficit monetization and these recurring shocks had built up pressures that finally forced a reckoning in 1991, the subject of the next lesson.
